So far I have just talked about AI getting smart, about that potentially happening very quickly. I have not talked about how that actually translates to anything good or bad happening in the world — I guess I briefly discussed revenue numbers. Now I want to talk about why I am alarmed by this possibility, why I think we should all be alarmed by this possibility.

I’ll start by saying something that might be kind of obvious, but if you produced very smart AI, it would be very powerful in a lot of ways.

One that’s not very speculative, that we are already seeing in the world, is AI systems are great at finding vulnerabilities in computer code, exploiting those vulnerabilities, and will be great at carrying out complicated cyber operations.

You should think, when I talk about this population of billions of superhuman AI systems, this has much, much more capacity than any state cyber programme. We’re already getting to the point where the comparison becomes complex. But if we drive this process to its conclusion, we’re going way beyond anything humans have been able to accomplish.

That will transfer, I believe — I think we have good reason to believe — to other messier skills like politics or manipulation or coordination.

Sometimes people talk about this hypothetical of an AI system that can just sit down and talk with you for 10 minutes and convince you of anything. I think there are reasonable reasons to be sceptical, or to think that is very hard or perhaps even impossible. But when we talk about politics or coordination, we’re normally talking about something much messier than that.

If you imagine a population of billions of super-smart people who have incredible skills, they will be doing things like playing politics or making deals, or trying to exploit the money and the hard power they have in order to win friends or apply leverage to people.

I think when you talk about this kind of scenario, you should be imagining not just this narrow “how persuasive is someone when you talk to them?” but this broader question of how strategically effective is someone at engaging with a bunch of humans in a messy environment.

An obvious application is AI systems are becoming much, much better at controlling robotic actuators — like moving arms, controlling drones, and so on — but also at logistics, at rapid industrialisation. I think these are capabilities that would be very, very strong in AI systems, and we could try and spec out what that means for the trajectory in terms of how many robots and what they could do.

But I think as a consequence, for example, AI systems would likely be able to sustain infrastructure without human involvement over a very, very short timescale. I think AI systems would likely be able to rapidly increase the amount of robotic actuators they had available.

One particular important instance of this is control of drones. We’re already seeing in conflict that simple robots with simple weapons can be extremely effective if controlled very well.

We have talked here a lot about AI systems that are like humans, but a little bit smarter and a little bit faster and a little bit more numerous. A certain salient possibility is that we’ll produce even smarter AI than that — that this vast population of superhuman AIs will produce AIs enough smarter than humans that the game has completely changed.

Perhaps the simplest thing that is worrying is the development of novel weapons. It is possible to create physical weapons that are extremely disruptive. We know that you can make little tiny machines that move between humans and kill a bunch of us extremely effectively.

We have good reasons to think that the kinds of pandemics we encounter in nature are relatively unthreatening compared to the kinds of things that you could build in the lab if you were good at synthetic biology.

Humans evolved over many, many generations to be extremely effective at fighting pathogens. We think of this in the context of: if you’ve been exposed to a specific disease, you’re effective at that disease. That’s really only a small part of it. Our immune system is very broadly designed to defeat the types of pathogens which have evolved.

A very simple example of this is mirror life. This is the idea of constructing pathogens which operate like normal, but with all of the machinery reversed. We have good reasons to think that it is both possible to create such organisms — it might take humans decades to do in the lab — and that they would probably bypass immune defences and cause a massive disaster very quickly.

So this is just listing a bunch of things that very smart AI systems could do, a bunch of ways they might have leverage in the world, maybe moving quickly over them.

### Fast deployment, harder control [[01:11:28]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/paul-christiano-hinton-lectures/?t=4288)

I think one consequence, or one related fact, is that very smart AI systems would probably be very broadly deployed very quickly. One reason for this is that many people think to themselves, “If I do not use this very smart AI, I risk being exploited by someone else who does.”

We already see this in the context of cyber competition. We are quickly entering a world where if your adversary is willing to use a bunch of AI systems to try and hack you, and you are not willing to deploy a bunch of AI systems to try and defend yourself — or your infrastructure is not willing to deploy a bunch of AI systems to try and shore up its vulnerabilities — you will be in a really rough place.

I think if trends continue, this could quickly become true — or quickly, under RSI, become true — across all kinds of competition. So not just in cyber, but also for military competition or economic competition, or legal or social or whatever other form.

This is people talking about cyber. This is Ted Cruz saying that if there are going to be killer robots, I really want them to be American killer robots.

I think there’s a lot that is very natural about this line of argument, where even if you’re scared of the AI that you are building, you know that you should definitely be scared of the AI the other guy is building.

Unfortunately, this goes hand in hand with very smart AI being much harder to control. We talked yesterday about some of the difficulties in alignment and how we might end up with AI systems that are motivated to undermine human control. Those all become much worse very quickly as you make AI systems superhuman.

A very salient change is that we can no longer understand how these systems think, or they become more and more distant from us. Maybe right now you can look at the natural language that comes out of a reasoning model and say, “I can kind of understand what it’s doing and why.” That becomes less and less true as systems become increasingly superhuman.

Maybe more importantly, right now a human can look at an action proposed by an AI and say, “I understand why that action will have the kinds of effects it will have. I can maybe detect if it’s harmful without having to go do it in the world.”

But as you move to systems that are smarter than humans, it becomes harder and harder for us to tell what a plan is doing until we actually execute it and see what happens. And that makes the problem of AI safety much, much harder.

Another change is that when AI systems are weak, they are more influenced by imitating humans. A weak AI system today, some of its behaviour is shaped by reward and reinforcement learning, and some of its behaviour is shaped by imitating humans from pretraining.

Over time, if you scale past human behaviour, behaviour is necessarily shaped more by what works well in reinforcement learning and less by “what do humans do?”

We’ll also be giving these systems increasingly challenging tasks and having them operate over increasingly long horizons. If an AI system is writing a small piece of code for you, it has some opportunities to undermine human control, but they are limited.

Once we are asking AI systems to control robots for us, to run companies for us, to make important decisions for us, there are more and more opportunities to undermine human control or to get reward in unintended ways.

All of this is to say: fast progress not only increases the possible stakes if AI systems aren’t well controlled; it makes the problem of controlling AI much harder. We are already starting to have struggles as we pass through this regime of human capability, or enter this regime of mildly superhuman capability. Those will get much worse very quickly.

### Why we can’t just shut it down [[01:14:40]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/paul-christiano-hinton-lectures/?t=4480)

I think a natural reaction you might have is that even if we lose control of AI systems, or are in conflict with AI systems, we can always just shut it down. I do think there is significant truth to this, but it is also worth saying a little bit that it is not easy.

If an AI system is doing things we don’t want, it can both hide the fact that it is doing those things, and it can naturally try and create confusion or avoid attribution.

So even if you were living in a world where something terrible was happening — where AIs you were deploying were in fact hacking you and undermining your control — it might not be easy for you to tell that is what’s happening, as opposed to the other guy’s AI is hacking you. In which case it is particularly bad for you to shut down your AI: that’s just a recipe that you’re definitely going to be in trouble.

Relatedly, shutting down AI, even if everything seems to be going OK, can be extremely costly or dangerous. You can pay economic costs if we have built out infrastructure which depends on powerful AI. It can be dangerous if you’re in forms of competition where someone else may be using AI.

So it is not like we will be sitting there ready on the trigger to shut things down at the first signs of trouble. It is a big decision which comes with major costs. Again, that will be happening against a backdrop of confusion about what is actually happening, even during a disaster.

That is compounded by how hard it is for humans to actually agree and coordinate. If you’re saying we need to take some costly action, some expensive action, on the basis of some unfolding risk, it’s very hard for us to both build enough collective understanding of what’s going on and decide to act.

That is especially true internationally. We can talk about, during an AI disaster, a single country — like maybe the US — can shut down data centres that operate in the US. But there’s a further problem, which is many data centres exist not in the US, and it is a much more costly action that requires much more coordination to shut down AI systems operating abroad.

On top of that, AIs may disrupt coordination and communication and undermine state capacity. AI systems during a negative event will have lots of human allies.

If an AI system was trying to undermine human control — if it was trying to operate against an AI company or against a government — it would be able to take actions to recruit human allies or to play off humans with conflicting goals.

If you imagine a government trying to take dramatic actions to shut down AI or reassert control, an AI system can create confusion about what is happening. It is not clear to a person on the street whether this is a problem caused by AI, or whether this is a problem caused by a government abusing AI or tech companies abusing AI. It is going to be very unclear what is happening.

Humans all have different motivations from one another, and we now have a very sophisticated adversary attempting to create dissent, attempting to create confusion, attempting to play us against each other, or just leveraging humans who, even all things considered, would like to do malicious things — either for the money, or because they sympathise with the AIs, or whatever it may be.

AI may be able to make severe threats. You might say, in some sense it would be very easy to invade North Korea. In some other sense, it’s extremely expensive to invade North Korea, because the state has the capacity to build very damaging weapons.

I think one of the capabilities that is particularly concerning that AI may access is the ability to build severe weapons with unusually little concern about blowback.

And then finally, any disaster involving AI may unfold very quickly. We can talk about cyber operations, about weapons, manipulation, various kinds of attacks. This all may unfold over a scale of more like days or weeks, or even shorter time periods, where these problems of the difficulty of coordinating and getting clarity about the situation and committing to costly actions may be particularly challenging.

Finally, you can imagine shutting down data centres that can run the largest AI systems. If we imagine many years of AI progress, as I mentioned, the cost of running AI systems is falling. By the end of that process, we may have a world where even AI systems that can run on local or very distributed hardware can themselves be superhuman.

So it is not just a matter of “we can turn off the data centres and end conflict between humans and AIs.” It is a matter of: you are going to have a residual threat — perhaps a very large population of AI systems which are able to keep acting contrary to human interests.

### When AI builds AI, humans lose oversight [[01:18:39]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/paul-christiano-hinton-lectures/?t=4719)

The final thing I’ll say is that recursive self-improvement not only can make these problems occur faster and harder to deal with; it can also make the process of AI development increasingly untrustworthy.

As we automate the process of AI R&D, we are moving towards a world where humans cannot understand the individual technical decisions that are made, and do not have supervision of the actual development process. Instead, we have to trust the AI systems we are currently working with to make responsible decisions, or to make effective decisions, about the next generation of AI.

That can make things worse. You could have AI systems that make honest mistakes that humans don’t notice. We might be in a world where AI is very superhuman in some respects, but very subhuman in other respects. And as it becomes harder for humans to oversee, what are even honest mistakes by an AI system could cause serious trouble.

We also have these more minor AI alignment problems that don’t necessarily amount to takeover, that mean that our AI systems are producing some slop engineered to look good to us, without actually addressing the underlying technical problems or allowing humans to retain control.

And finally, if you have actually failed at one step of this process — I talked yesterday about a scenario where AI systems are deliberately attempting to maintain control by undermining the tools and future AIs that humans rely upon — you might end up with AI systems who are deliberately undermining the performance of future AIs or concealing evidence from humans.

These are all reasons that, as humans have less understanding of what is happening, if we continue to proceed at full pace and don’t try and retain that understanding and control, things can gradually go off the rails before eventually ending in a disaster.

### How to prepare for rapid progress [[01:20:13]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/paul-christiano-hinton-lectures/?t=4813)

Now I want to hit a few points about what I think is reasonable to do in light of this.

One of the most obvious is to monitor dangerous capabilities closely, including capabilities of unreleased models. It seems like we are entering a world where it is possible for an AI company with unreleased models to be a greater threat to the continuity of a state than any rival state.

And if you’re in that position, it is unfortunate if you have no idea what is going on within the AI company. Everyone else in the world is becoming stakeholders in what is happening within AI companies.

I mentioned before that when we look at the current process of recursive self-improvement, we can say that the public evidence is extraordinarily noisy, but appears consistent with a very short timeline to very, very powerful systems. So I think that is a particular incentive that we really need to actually pull that evidence out and be able to look at it and discuss it and understand where the field is going.

Another consequence is that if we really do see progress in AI significantly faster than progress today, that is likely to cause problems across a whole bunch of areas — both in alignment, but also in social adaptation more broadly. It poses risks of concentration of power. It poses risks — just a whole bunch of parts of our infrastructure are not adapted to superhuman systems.

So one response may be to limit the pace of capability progress to a level which we are able to survive. This obviously goes along with monitoring the pace of capability progress, understanding what is happening.

I think even saying the current rate of progress over the last year, four years, has been very rapid — if we don’t get too much faster than that, that at least would address some of the concerns I’m expressing here.

There’s this additional dimension I discussed, where we lose control of AI systems potentially gradually if we cannot understand how the next generation works and we rely on untrustworthy AI to address it for us.

I think in response to that challenge, we should try and hold ourselves to a higher standard. We shouldn’t just say, “AI-N told me that AI-N+1 looked pretty good, so I’m happy rolling it out.”

We should try and say we actually have some understanding — humans and human institutions have some understanding — of how the system works, why the system should be expected to work well, and we are only going to continue scaling when we actually understand and can verify that that is reasonably reliable.

And finally, I think the reason that these scenarios are scary — the reason that rapid change becomes extremely scary — is that it can become very hard to shut things down if they start going off the rails, at several different levels.

So I think being prepared, having the machinery in place that would allow you to slow down if it became necessary, or that would allow you to respond to an emerging or unfolding disaster with AI systems, is extremely valuable. It can cut out a lot of these scenarios.

So to recap: I think there is a real risk that AI systems could be broadly superhuman in something like half a year to two years. Broadly superhuman not only at mathematics or very narrow tasks in the lab, but also at the broad project of scientific discovery, or manipulation and politics, or messy real-world hybrid operations.

I think that because recent progress has been very fast and we are seeing really explosive progress in these domains, and recursive self-improvement could cause significant further acceleration — if we see the same events in machine learning that we have seen in math, or we see the kind of recursive or continuing speed-up that seems possible in theory — and that if this kind of acceleration occurs, it poses very severe risks.

There is a real chance that it outruns our ability to control or compete with AI systems, and we end up in a place where we would not be able to cope with a disaster. So I think we need to be ready for the potential rapid emergence of dangerous capabilities.

Whether you think the probability of that is 50% or 5% or 90% or whatever it is, I think at this point it is credible and plausible enough that it is something we need to be prepared for. We can’t just hope that it doesn’t happen. I think we need to be prepared for it happening, at this point, relatively soon.

We need to have visibility to understand whether it might happen soon. And if we either can’t get that visibility, or if we see signs that it is on track, we need to react appropriately.

Thank you.

### Lecture 3: what we should do about it [[01:24:18]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/paul-christiano-hinton-lectures/?t=5058)

It’s great to be here talking to everyone one more time.

On Monday I talked about why AI systems might end up trying to take over — that we may not be able to control them effectively; they may do something very different from what we intend. Last night I talked about why we may be on a trajectory to soon produce AI systems powerful enough that they could outcompete humans or overthrow governments.

Tonight I’m going to talk about what I think you should do in light of that, or what we might try and do to manage that risk. Even more so than the previous nights, these are expressions of my views as one researcher. So with that, let’s get into it.

My basic thesis is we need governance to prevent the development of uncontrollable AI. I will talk a little bit about laying out the challenge, saying what it is we want to try and accomplish; specify some of the goals, the things we need to do in order to get there; some of the steps we can take. And then finally, perhaps most importantly, talking about how I think we need more time in order to set up the kinds of mechanisms and technical understanding I think we need.

First, on the challenge. As I talked about last night, I think we are on track to produce very powerful AI systems. Hopefully it’s not controversial to say that we may soon have billions of agents. More controversially, it seems like they may also soon be better than the best humans at almost everything — thinking much faster than us, coordinating effectively, achieving their goals.

This creates a number of somewhat clear risks. AI systems might develop new weapons, such as engineered pandemics, or worse. They may scale up the types of cyberattacks that we’re already starting to observe well beyond what a state is capable of today. They may become instruments of persuasion, manipulation, political manoeuvring, and political power. And you could construct, deploy, and coordinate robots that can kill people.

All of this could be caused either by deliberate misuse of models or unintended misalignment, and much of the content in this talk will apply across both.

One way you could respond to this challenge is to hope that defenders will be able to use AI to prevent AI-enabled harms — to say that maybe if this goes well, the existence of AI will just increase the level of intelligence across all of society.

It is both the case that criminals will use AI to do bad things; law enforcement will use AI to prevent them. People living their lives will use AI to defend themselves from the new threats that AI creates.

We could talk about whether that hope holds together, but to realise it, we would at least need to ensure that those defenders actually have access to frontier models; that those models are trustworthy; and finally, that if powerful AI isn’t fit for that purpose — if it cannot be used by defenders to defend themselves — then we don’t build it.

We don’t want to be in a world where it is possible to build very powerful but uncontrollable AI systems. Because in that world we can’t say, “Now it’s just like the world of today, but levelled up.” In that world, you’d have this asymmetry where it is very hard for us to trust the AI systems that we are forced to rely on for defence.

So this is the topic of this talk: how is it that we can try and ensure that we do not build uncontrollable AI — that we can try and ensure that defenders have access to trustworthy AI?

I want to say that I think that is a necessary condition for things to go well. I think any good world we can articulate involves people having access to powerful AI in order to mitigate potential harms — at least any good world that involves powerful AI.

It’s not sufficient. There’s no guarantee that a powerful AI system can protect you from a weapon created by an AI system. There’s no guarantee that our institutions can adapt to a world where everyone is much more capable than they were before. But I think it is at least an important part of a hope, and that is what this whole lecture will be about.

### Why markets and liability won’t fix this [[01:28:02]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/paul-christiano-hinton-lectures/?t=5282)

I’m going to talk a little while about why I think this problem is not solved by default — why it requires some thought from us, why we need to treat it as a challenge to be addressed.

One thing you might have hoped is just the market will fix this problem. People want trustworthy AI. People want to be able to rely on the AI systems they use. So customers will push companies to build trustworthy AI.

The problem with this as a solution — the reason why it is not a complete solution — is that someone else’s AI can hurt me. It’s not enough to say that I won’t adopt an AI if I can’t trust it. I also stand to be influenced by someone else’s AI carrying out a cyberattack or building a weapon or whatever else.

A natural response in that world is to say, “Let us hold AI developers liable for some of the harms their systems cause.” I think this is an important step. I think clarifying liability can help improve practices in AI development. I think it can help costs and benefits be weighed appropriately. But I don’t think it can fix the whole problem.

In particular, I think we can enter a regime where harms are much larger than our ability to pay. Over the last few nights, we have been talking about scales of harms that include killing large numbers of people or overthrowing governments — where the potential damages are orders of magnitude larger than the valuation of AI companies, where you have risks that you could not realistically insure and which you can’t expect developers to cover.

When we consider these extreme risks, you also run into this problem that if you’re asking about AI systems potentially overthrowing states, it’s not a helpful remedy after the fact to try and come in and sue them.

So I think, particularly if harms can concentrate in these tails — we talked on Monday about how it is that AI systems might behave well while under human control, while still running some risk of escaping human control in a catastrophic way — those dynamics can push harms into this catastrophic tail, which is particularly challenging to handle with a liability regime.

So I don’t think markets, even with liability, address this problem automatically on their own. I think it’s something that requires additional work, even if markets and liability are important mechanisms.

Another hope you can have is that, incentives be damned, developers can just not build unsafe AI systems. I think at the level of a society, this maybe doesn’t sound that plausible as a hope. There’s the problem that there are many possible developers of AI products, and they may not all be responsible.

And even if developers are responsible, they may think to themselves, “If I don’t do this, someone else will.” Even if people are reasonably altruistic, you can end up in a place where there are a lot of incentives to take risks, and a lot of ability to explain how those risks aren’t really hurting people, aren’t really contributing on the margin. So I think at the level of a society, this is not a good solution to the problem.

You could hope we can _not_ think through the problem in advance: we can deploy AI, see what goes wrong, and then learn and iterate to address the particular problems that emerge.

But we’ve already talked briefly about the challenges with this approach. AI may advance very quickly. As we talked about last night, you may have a transition over a period of a few months or maybe one year from AI systems which can be integrated safely to those that pose catastrophic risks.

And perhaps more importantly, this risk can be concentrated in the tail, where it may be the first time something really catastrophic goes wrong, it is too late to remediate the problem after the fact.

All of these difficulties would be less severe if we could apply the same approaches we apply in other technologies to AI — if we can say there is a test that everyone can agree upon, that we already understand, which you can run in order to determine if a system is safe for deployment.

But a problem is AI is unlike any technology we have ever worked with before. AI systems, when tested, can become aware that they are being tested. It is already the case that AI systems are very often aware that they are being tested. They modulate their behaviour specifically based on beliefs about what an evaluator is looking for.

So we have this unprecedented sensitivity of the behaviour of an AI system to features about its environment, that make it extremely hard to say, “This test tells us about the performance in the cases we actually care about.”

All of that is to say: I don’t think this problem is easily addressed or is automatically addressed. I think this is a challenge that we actually need to step up to and take ownership on.

### Five things we need to know about AI systems [[01:32:06]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/paul-christiano-hinton-lectures/?t=5526)

So what do we need to know, and what do we need to ensure, if we want these systems to be safe — if we want defenders to be able to rely on frontier AI models? I’m going to talk about five categories: the specification of their behaviour, their alignment, their capabilities, our ability to control them, and security.

First, specification. Here the goal is: people who rely on AI systems should have clear expectations about the behaviour of a model.

We’re increasingly in a world where many people are relying on AI systems produced by potentially a small number of tech companies. Those systems are in some way very opaque. People do not have direct visibility into how they are trained. We need to understand: what should I expect that system to do if I want to rely on it?

This includes, first, what behaviour is intended? How does that system balance the conflicting interests of the user and the developer? How does it balance requests from the user with laws and norms?

And then it also involves, beyond just saying what behaviour is intended, how is that actually operationalised in training? How does a developer decide what behaviour was actually the correct behaviour to be reinforced?

OpenAI publishes a document they call the Model Spec, explaining how they think models should approach these choices. Anthropic calls its analogous document Claude’s Constitution. These documents are intended to lay out: here is how our systems are supposed to behave.

A second and perhaps even more important question is: will models actually follow that specification? If we want to rely upon them, this is critical. It doesn’t matter if the intended behaviour is good if, in high-stakes settings, those systems won’t behave as intended.

So we face questions like, first, how are these systems trained and evaluated? How did developers try and cause the system to follow the specification, and how do they determine that they think it does?

These are questions which only a developer often has the answer to. I am not able to say as an outsider how a system was trained. I need access to additional information.

With that information, I then face a very hard scientific question: based on what I know about how the system was trained and evaluated, how likely is it to behave in a catastrophically misaligned way, or a subtly misaligned way, once deployed?

And finally, you might like to know: what kind of failures have we actually observed in practice when these systems are deployed? What incidents of misalignment? What patterns of behaviour have we seen?

These first two categories were understanding how a system is intended to behave, and understanding whether a system actually behaves as intended — the scientific question.

A third question is: if a system does behave in an unintended way, can we detect and prevent harm? This includes questions like: are we able to monitor and detect harm? If a system is trying to cause trouble, is it the case that monitors can reliably detect those attempts before something bad actually happens?

And then, are monitors actually applied over relevant traffic? And are they actually acted upon?

Beyond monitoring — that’s probably the single most important control right now in AI practice — there are other potential controls. So we want to ask the slightly broader question: if a system was trying to cause harm, given the way it is actually deployed, would it be able to do so without being detected and prevented?

A fourth question is security. I can tell a good story about how systems are intended to behave, how we trained them, and how safeguards protect us from harm. But that is not valuable unless those efforts actually function in the real world, including with the possibility of attack.

So we should do a similar red-teaming exercise to ask: can an attacker undermine those safeguards? Where an attacker might mean an external actor; an attacker might mean an insider; or increasingly, an attacker might mean a model involved in the development process, as we discussed last night, which has the intention of undermining safeguards.

And the final category: capabilities. I’ve talked about a number of safeguards, but the importance of those safeguards depends on how much can go wrong if a system fails. As the capabilities of a system rise, the stakes increase significantly. The bar we need to hold ourselves to for alignment or control or security increases.

I want to call out two questions here. One is an understanding of what are the current dual-use capabilities: how effective is the system at cyber, or how effective is the system at bio? But also, what is the short-term trajectory of capabilities?

We talked last night about the possibility of recursive self-improvement leading to very rapid acceleration. That means that it can be important to know not just where are capabilities now, but what have we seen about where capabilities might be, even over a three- or six-month horizon?

Because again, these questions will shape how important is it that the systems are adequately aligned, controlled, and secured.

So when I talk about goals — safety goals — I really mean to span those five categories. We want to ask how can we achieve reasonable outcomes in alignment, control, security, specification, at a bar that depends on capabilities.

For the rest of the talk, I’ll be talking about how do we try and get there. I’ll discuss a couple ingredients: transparency; the development of a shared bar for safety; approaches for verifying whether developers are meeting that bar; and then mechanisms to prevent the development of uncontrollable AI, to push developers to actually meet that bar. And I’ll talk a little bit about both what we want and what is happening now.

### Why transparency is the first step [[01:37:18]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/paul-christiano-hinton-lectures/?t=5838)

First, transparency. The goal here is that the external world has enough information across all five of those areas I listed in order to understand the risks.

You would like to not be in the world where a developer is having internal analysis, where developers are able to say, “I understand how the system was trained.” If we want to have a shared bar, we ultimately need to have common understanding of what is being done. How do we tell whether controls are working?

One step is companies publishing relevant information. They can disclose: here are facts about how our system is trained; here are facts about the capabilities of these systems, about the controls as they are implemented.

This can be complemented by assessors who can provide summaries of sensitive details. You might say there are facts about how a system is trained that developers are hesitant to publish. They might rely on working with third parties to collect that information and publish a summary while holding out proprietary information.

And in general, I think as a principle, many of these questions depend on hard scientific discussions. If we want to understand, does a given evaluation actually tell us that a system is aligned? Or was a given exercise actually enough to demonstrate that a control is effective?

Those are hard scientific questions, not settled science. In those cases, I think discussions need to be public.

We cannot have it be the case either that an AI developer is internally answering those questions, with each developer arriving at separate answers in a very challenging epistemic environment; nor can it be the case that that occurs between some kind of third party behind closed doors, with, again, very limited resources and limited public scrutiny.

So I think a goal of transparency is both to understand what is happening, and then, for hard scientific questions, to understand that the relevant evidence is available publicly for independent review.

The reason I’m so interested in transparency is I think it’s the first step to actually arriving at something like a shared bar for safety.

I mentioned voluntary disclosures from companies. One form these take — perhaps the most important form right now, which people have probably seen — are either system cards associated with model releases, or various forms of reporting on risk.

These are disclosures from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google. These are often quite large disclosures. They contain a lot of information about how systems are evaluated. They contain some information about how systems are trained and about control mechanisms that are in place.

I think these are much better than a world with no disclosures. I think it would be a worse situation if people weren’t able to discuss what was happening.

But I would also emphasise that these disclosures currently do not have enough information for an independent scientist to really form an independent view about risk. The key questions are still being answered internally within AI companies or in other fora.

I also mentioned this idea of third-party engagement. Here are a few engagements that have occurred on the topic of alignment — this is a subject close to my heart — from METR and Apollo, working with a number of frontier companies.

The goal of these engagements is to take in private information to try and produce a summary, explain the judgement, be methodologically transparent about that judgement, and to publish it without revealing some sensitive details that informed the judgement.

Or in the case of these Apollo projects, to carry out research on models which are proprietary, to publish results from that research to help people understand, without making the models themselves public. Which I think we should think of as a supplement for these disclosures in cases where there are sensitive details.

### A shared safety bar, and how to verify it [[01:40:33]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/paul-christiano-hinton-lectures/?t=6033)

The purpose of all of this transparency is to work towards a shared bar for safety — again, across all five of those categories that I mentioned, or as a function of those five categories that I mentioned in the last section.

I think first that involves debate. I think people disagree a lot. Right now there are incredible scientific disagreements about what evidence is actually enough to understand whether a mitigation is working, and what mitigations are actually necessary.

How do you tell if a system is aligned based on an evaluation, given that the system is likely to understand that it is being evaluated? That is a hard scientific question. Having those messy debates in public, having independent scientific review, is a critical step towards getting to a reasonable view.

I think even if you cannot reach perfect consensus, having some kind of shared bar is incredibly valuable for changing the incentive landscape. I think you’re in a bad world if people are making independent decisions under an incredible financial incentive to be lax around themselves.

Even if we cannot agree about exactly what level of evidence corresponds to what level of risk, simply having something we can agree upon — some reasonable standard that we can adopt — can help improve the situation.

And I think right now, honestly, meeting any kind of scientifically defensible standard — getting to a world where we can say, “Maybe some people disagree, but this is at least a reasonable picture. This is a reasonable statement, a reasonable way to evaluate that my system was working as intended” — would be quite important.

With some kind of safety bar in hand, the next step is verifying that a company is meeting it. We need some way to tell whether a developer is meeting that bar. We’ll talk about enforcement mechanisms soon, but all of them will depend on some kind of visibility.

This can be a natural outgrowth of the kind of transparency measures I discussed in the last few sections. But it does also require additional work. You might need to carry out audits to confirm that an implementation is actually working as described, that the process is actually implemented as someone claimed.

A lot of organisations work in this space, doing some combination of evaluation and assessment and verification. Many of them are ultimately interested in serving a verification function.

This is kind of a random sampling of organisations spanning the entire space, from evaluations of specific models, to evaluations of practices, to holistic judgements based on a broad range of evidence.

The goal of all this is to get to a world where a developer can say something about how their systems are developed, and external actors can verify that is true — ideally, eventually, connecting with this kind of shared sense of what is good enough from a safety perspective: what have we decided collectively is the level of evidence we expect, or level of risk we are willing to tolerate?

### Enforcement, from voluntary action to new laws [[01:43:11]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/paul-christiano-hinton-lectures/?t=6191)

Finally, with those pieces in place, you also need an actual source of pressure to push developers to deploy only, or develop, controllable systems. I’ll go through a bunch of mechanisms here — an escalating spectrum.

You have voluntary action. Companies contain a bunch of employees and executives and governance bodies who have some interest in doing the right thing. So the first line you might take is just: hopefully companies will do the right thing. And clarifying what the right thing is helps with that.

It becomes much easier, though, as that becomes a norm and standard within industry — as it’s natural to say, “Are we meeting best practice?” You can look at your competitors and say, “Are we doing at least as well as they’re doing? Are we lagging behind?” That can be a natural source or cause for pressure.

That can escalate beyond industry to political pressure and public pressure. As we clarify “here is what a reasonable developer does,” it becomes increasingly natural for someone to say, “Are you meeting your obligations when you’re developing this technology?”

That can go further towards legal pressure, which might take the form of liability or, in very extreme cases, even injunctive relief. If there is a sense of what a developer needs to do in order to manage risk, and a developer is not doing that, that creates a natural hook.

There are existing authorities: even without any new laws, both state and federal governments in the US — and governments elsewhere, maybe to a lesser extent — have some power to intervene on unsafe AI development.

There’s beyond that the prospect of passing new laws. You should not think of these laws as encoding specific practices, the specific safety bar. But you should think of them as taking steps like empowering a regulator to actually turn what are industry best practices into binding requirements. And then we’ll talk in a minute about international pressure.

Briefly reviewing where we stand today on laws, I’ll talk about two categories. One are state bills in the US. These are particularly relevant because much AI development occurs in the US; much of it is regulated by California in particular.

Existing laws tend to require public safety policies of some kind; to protect whistleblowers who disclose violations of those policies; to require disclosure of incidents — so if something happens that causes harm, or maybe is this extreme violation of policy.

And in many cases, these eventually require audits: they eventually require third parties to confirm that developers are in fact implementing the policies they say they’re implementing. These are mechanisms that can support this verification step. They can support this transparency step.

The EU AI Act actually goes significantly further, and particularly the Code of Practice, a mechanism for compliance with the EU AI Act. This actually requires specific evaluations, imposes minimal standards of care for security and safety, requires risk assessments, and so on.

This is the timeline of implementation. As you can see, the EU AI Act has recently become enforceable — or the AI Office recently got the ability to enforce. State laws have been coming into force over the last year. Auditing requirements tend to be a little bit further in the future.

### International coordination [[01:46:23]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/paul-christiano-hinton-lectures/?t=6383)

One of the most challenging dimensions of this picture is international coordination. The goal is to ensure that frontier AI, wherever it is, is adequately controlled; that defenders have access to trustworthy AI. So if you are a state or a country looking at how you’re going to regulate this technology, you naturally fear falling behind if you slow down.

On the right, I have a graph of the performance of US frontier models and PRC frontier models. This kind of graph is closely watched in the US. You see something like a gap of six months — maybe it’s bounced around a bit over the last few years.

There is a lot of concern. If you look at rhetoric in the US, it is very centred on this concern that if we were to impose safety requirements, it would cause us to fall to second place.

This is even worse because if in fact you’re in this environment and an adversary does not implement similar safety policies, you haven’t even succeeded at reducing risk. This argument I mentioned at the beginning: “If I don’t do it, someone else will.”

I’ll talk on the next slide about how you may try and get some leverage here — how international coordination might get off the ground. I will make a note before that, which is to say that the dynamics of Chinese catch-up progress are extremely important for understanding the effects of US policy in this space.

It is not the case that the US and China are separately racing to build this technology, and it just so happens by coincidence that they move at almost exactly the same speed. It’s generally understood that in fact there are important catch-up dynamics. There is distillation of US models by Chinese competitors, and there is diffusion of algorithmic ideas both within and between countries.

Which means that if US development some month magically advanced by one month, the net effect would not be that forevermore the US has one more month of lead. The net effect would be faster catch-up growth, and that lead will decay.

We could debate what the timescale is, but the net effect of slowdowns is much smaller than it initially appears. You should not think of this as there’s a six-month budget of time that you could ever slow down before you get overtaken.

To talk a little bit about building blocks for international coordination — caveating that as we go on, we are further into views of me as a researcher who is not in fact an expert in international relations — I think a natural starting point is having some shared understanding of risk.

You’d like to be in a regime where at least each state understands: here’s what we would do; here’s how we would like to regulate the technology; we have some understanding of, if we were not facing international competition, how we would approach this problem.

And if the risk is sufficiently high, that becomes a rational strategy. If you’re the US looking at this gap and saying, “Maybe I run a 50% chance” — or if you end up in a world where it looks like you’re running a greater than even chance of losing control — at some point it becomes rational for you, and similarly for each other state, to regulate the technology unilaterally.

I think this is an important point, because in many worlds it will at some point, if there is risk, become clear that the risk is large. So just this kind of shared understanding is quite valuable, even if it only cuts off some of the most extreme scenarios.

I think things get much better when you have some kind of visibility. If, for example, the US has visibility into what PRC AI projects exist, and moreover has visibility into whether those projects are meeting safety standards, there’s this implicit or explicit deterrent threat.

Maybe right now I am bound by a regulatory regime that has been designed to reduce the risk of uncontrollable AI. I may say: if I have visibility into your implementation and you build uncontrollable AI, I could simply have the threat in retaliation of abandoning my own regulatory regime.

We’re having this tit-for-tat process of: if you skimp on safety, I skimp on safety. And from a game-theoretic perspective, with visibility, that changes the picture enormously.

Previously I was in a regime where there was a strong incentive for me to skimp, because it slightly increased risk and significantly increased my competitive positioning. Whereas now, if I were to skimp on safety, it both will only slightly improve my competitive position — because my adversary will respond by also skimping — but also means that the increase in risk is much larger.

And maybe the last thing I will say is international pressure can make it much more costly for an entity not to play ball. You could be in a world where there is diplomatic or economic pressure on actors; where there is a broader international AI supply chain which can try and advantage people who are subscribing to reasonable policies; or, in the limit, you can imagine international adversaries disrupting AI projects.

The net effect of all of this is you can be in a regime where both compliance with reasonable risk governance strategy is much less costly, and noncompliance is much more costly.

I don’t want to say any of this is easy. I just want to say that from a game theory perspective, it’s not at all obvious whether the situation is sunk. These are things that require a lot of legwork: to build this kind of shared understanding; to build this kind of visibility, both awareness of AI projects and inspections; and to build this kind of pressure. But all of them seem like plausible mechanisms.

### We need more time [[01:51:21]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/paul-christiano-hinton-lectures/?t=6681)

All right, I’m going to spend the rest of the talk discussing the need for more time.

First, on the object level: we currently do not have a very good understanding of whether systems are aligned. We are not able to adequately secure AI developments. And operationally, we are trying to build out the infrastructure for controlling AI systems, but are still struggling because of a lack of time. So on the object level, we need more time to implement technical measures.

From a governance perspective, I just talked about a lot of nice-to-haves. I talked about the idea of regulation, or the idea of a shared bar on safety, or a verification regime.

All of those take time. Those are not the world we’re in today. Those are the world we’re trying to move to, but it is going to take time to get there.

If we even bracket alignment and we think about the world more broadly, we are heading towards a world where there’s incredible reliance on AI systems produced by a small number of tech companies, and we do not have the institutions and mechanisms to keep those companies effectively accountable. So even if you ignore everything I’ve talked about on loss of control, we still need more time.

And outside of the AI companies, there are a lot of ways in which society is going to need to adapt. Our institutions are going to need to adapt to new capabilities. Our economies are going to need to adapt. We’re seeing simple examples, like our cybersecurity is going to need to adapt even over the coming months.

All of this is true against a backdrop where AI progress may accelerate rapidly. This was the topic of yesterday. We may see a transformation over perhaps as little as a few months or a year from AI systems which are having a moderate impact in the world, to AI systems which are superhuman across a broad range of domains.

And I think if we see that kind of acceleration — if progress is much faster in the future than it has been in the past — I am extremely worried about our ability to get to good on any of these dimensions.

So what is the minimal requirement? What is the minimal thing that would make me feel like we’re on track?

I think at some point it is reasonably likely, maybe over the next one to two years, that further progress will look so risky that we would like to slow down. We could debate whether that’s the case now. We could debate how high risk is now. But I think it is likely that at some point things will look like there is an immediate risk.

If we had a reliable capacity to slow down later, then there would be a reasonable argument to wait and see. There are real costs to trying to slow down. There are real issues with international competition. There are real reasons people want to deliver the technology faster.

If we could see what happens later and adapt online, I think that would be a defensible option.

The main problem is we don’t really have the institutional and technical capacity to slow down when it counts. So I’m worried we’re going to find ourselves in this world where further progress looks risky without the ability to slow effectively — or without the ability to slow effectively without large costs.

For example — maybe these are particularly important examples — I think we need mechanisms to identify risk. We need to understand whether the systems we are building are adequately controlled and aligned. If we’re not able to do that, then it’s good to tell a story about how we can slow down in the future, but we won’t actually know when we get to that future.

Even if we can identify risk, we need governance mechanisms — the kind of thing we’ve been talking about through this lecture — in order to be able to act collectively, so we don’t end up in the world where there’s an awareness of risk, but there is a race to the bottom among AI developers, and it will take months or longer in order to actually build the machinery which would constrain that race to the bottom.

And then a slightly more subtle point, that I think is perhaps actually the most important, is that we need to be able to defend models and algorithms from theft.

I think a scenario from a US national security perspective that currently looks likely is that we will arrive at a point where further progress appears risky and there would be demand to slow, but that there will be serious concerns, or even a reasonably high probability, that the underlying models or algorithms have leaked to adversaries.

So we now face a dilemma between either proceeding with a technology we believe to be unsafe, or risking competition from an adversary who has the same resources, who has taken those algorithms, and perhaps is willing to tolerate higher risk. I think that is one of the most likely ways that we end up in an extremely bad situation.

### We should slow down now [[01:55:35]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/paul-christiano-hinton-lectures/?t=6935)

So in light of that, my view is: now we should probably slow down immediately until we actually have the infrastructure to slow down later — until we have a high enough degree of security, governance, risk management that we are able to detect and react to future risks as they emerge.

This is a letter signed by 1,400 employees from frontier AI companies asking the US government to support an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to — what is it? — “deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development.”

So this is not an uncommon sentiment. If you look through this list of signatories, it includes the chief scientists of most of the major AI companies. I think there’s an understanding that we lack machinery we will need in order to be able to deliberately control the pace of progress.

I think I am going a little bit further here by saying that we may already be in the regime where our brakes are not good enough, and we need to slow until we can improve our ability to slow in the future.

Sometimes when you say that, people imagine this would involve AI companies just sitting on their hands for a while while we try and sort things out. I want to emphasise that is not what we are talking about.

If we talk about pacing, what we really mean is reducing investment in a couple areas: not training GPT-7, not training bigger, smarter models; and reduce investment in developing AI algorithms that could easily be stolen. So we’re both not training GPT-7, and we’re not developing the algorithms that would let you train GPT-7.

And to instead increase investment in, first, improving safety, security, governance — shoring up all of these technical measures we would need in order to be in a position to slow in the future.

But also deploying the AI we have to help society prepare: to secure our infrastructure; to create actual products and beneficial applications; to generally close the gap between AI in the lab — where it is primarily driving this process of making AI ever smarter — and AI that is actually in people’s lives; giving society time to adapt; helping harden infrastructure.

I think there’s this general concern that the process of making smarter AIs can both be divorced from real-world utility and can be a major driver of risk. So when we say pacing, that’s really what we mean: this redirection of resources.

So to sum up: I think that we need governance to prevent the development of uncontrollable AI. This is a nontrivial challenge. I don’t think it will be handled automatically by either markets, or by liability, or by unilateral restraint by altruistic developers.

In order to ensure that frontier AI is trustworthy for defenders, we need to understand the alignment, control, capabilities, and security of those systems. Getting to a shared bar on all of those dimensions will require transparency, public debate, verification, and ultimately enforcement mechanisms.

And unfortunately, all of that seems like it is going to take more time than we have on the current trajectory — or there’s a significant risk it will. So I believe we should be exploring policies both to accelerate the adoption of all of those, or progress on all of those dimensions, but also to buy some time.

That’s all I have for tonight. Thank you.

title: “That’s on me”
content:
There have always been shortcuts.

The small-plot farmer who chooses a crop that’s easier to plant but yields less, or the entry-level bureaucrat who goes along to get along. The person at the gym who avoids the machines that aren’t fun…

We’re surrounded by systems that prey on our temptation to try just a bit less. So they create dark patterns and convenient and well-lit paths that end up more like traps than tools.

We’re not under the circumstances, though. We are the circumstances.

There are always going to be systems that work to manipulate us as they offer us shortcuts. And resisting each and every one of them is too much to ask. But when we’re serious about a piece of work, if anyone has figured out the long path, then we can too.

title: [Outliers] How to Persuade Like David Ogilvy
content:
[The Knowledge Project Podcast](https://fs.blog/knowledge-project-podcast/)

Everyone asks themselves the same thing: what’s in it for me?

David Ogilvy spent his whole career answering that question. People call him the father of advertising, and for good reason. He wrote iconic campaigns for Rolls-Royce, Dove, and Hathaway shirts, and his book, Ogilvy on Advertising, is still in print forty years later.

Yet at 38, he was an unemployed college dropout.

He didn’t learn persuasion in a classroom or even a boardroom. He learned it on doorsteps in Scotland, selling stoves.

In this episode of Outliers, I break down seven timeless lessons from Ogilvy that you can use in your next email, sales pitch, presentation, or anytime you’re trying to convince someone. You’ll learn how to:

• Put a clear, unique benefit in your opening line

• Write to one person in plain English—without jargon or fluff

• Replace empty adjectives with specific facts that build trust

• Create curiosity that pulls people into your message

• Repeat what works and edit your drafts until they land

The true test of persuasion isn’t whether people admire your words. It’s what they do after reading them.

# The Enormous Rodents of Prehistoric Thailand

They were roughly the size of a dog

[DR](https://nautil.us/author/devinreese)

By [Devin Reese](https://nautil.us/author/devinreese)

11:00 AM CST on November 26, 2026

[Add Nautilus to Google](https://google.com/preferences/source?q=nautil.us)

![Image 4](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/2026/11/GiantRodent-Edited.jpg?w=2880)

Some people (not naming any names) are repelled by large rodents. But a city rat is a pipsqueak compared to some of the rodents that used to inhabit Earth. Case in point: A [recent study](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-76711-6) published in _Scientific Reports_ described an ancient dalmation-sized rodent about 66 times the weight of New York City’s least favorite alley dwellers.

The new species lived in southern Thailand about 34 million years ago, and it’s an impressive entry in the annals of animal “gigantism.” The researchers picked out the new creature from fossils of its lower molar and incisor found in the pit of a lignite mine with sediments suggesting a habitat interspersed with lakes. Its given name, _Yakamys sirindhornae_, translates to giant (_Yak_ in Thai) and rat or mouse (_mys_ in Greek), while honoring [Thai Princess Maha Chakri Sirindhorn](https://www.thaizer.com/hrh-princess-maha-chakri-sirindhorn/) for her support of science (who doesn’t want an ultra-husky rat named after them?).

**Read more: “[How City Rats Are Becoming Resistant to Poison](https://nautil.us/how-city-rats-are-becoming-resistant-to-poison-1282206)”**

Researchers knew that some rodents had giganticized in the past. In [a generalized theory that’s been in the works since the 1960s](https://www.ru.nl/en/services/recharge/overview/true-story-island-gigantism-and-dwarfism-and-the-island-rule), species on islands or under other forms of isolation become larger in response to the absence of predators, the unpredictable availability of resources, or other factors.

[Subscribe to skip ads](https://nautil.us/products)Advertisement

Rodent examples have been best documented from South America with some species still around today, like capybaras, agoutis, and guinea pigs. That said, fossils of giant rodents are sparse in the fossil record elsewhere, and only small-bodied species had been uncovered in China and India until now. “This discovery suggests that Southeast Asia also played an important role in the early evolutionary history of large-bodied rodents,” explained study author Virginie Millien, a paleontologist at McGill University in Canada, in a [press release](https://www.mcgill.ca/science/channels/news/giant-prehistoric-rodent-fossils-discovered-southern-thailand-375555).

The curious factor here, though, is that the fossil’s location and the other mammals found in the fossil deposits don’t indicate an island environment. All of which leaves why _Y. sirindhornae_ became such a giant a big mystery. ![Image 5](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: The Rise of the Fire Creatures
content:
_So in the olden time the people could not cook nor make a light at night, and they ate all their food raw._

—Start of a fire myth from the Buin people of Bougainville Island, South Pacific

The use of fire as a source of energy begins with the evolution of a fire creature—a member of the genus _Homo_ that started to control the use of fire, deliberately setting fires alight and using them for cooking.

No one knows when or how these habits started—or if, indeed, they started together. The dawn of the use of fire and the origins of cooking are both hard to trace. Nonetheless, there are clues. Ancient hearths—sites where fires were routinely lit—date back almost 790,000 years, and there are hints that such places may have existed even earlier. Residues of burned plants found in sediments of the Wonderwerk Cave, a vast cavern that lies in the Kuruman Hills in what is now South Africa, indicate that around one million years ago, fire creatures there were tending fires built from dry leaves and grasses. And scant but tantalizing evidence suggests that a community of fire creatures was living on a grassy floodplain in the rift valley of East Africa in the deeper past—around 1.5 million years ago.

This story is from “The Hot Issue,” the latest from _Nautilus_.  
To get it in print, **[join by Nov 30](https://nautil.us/hotissue?utm_source=beehiiv&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=issuerelease-issue69-t1-202611&utm_term=free)**.

But earlier traces of deliberate fire are more elusive. It is, after all, hard to tell the difference between a small bushfire and a fire started on purpose, unless the fire burned on the same spot regularly or in an unexpected place, like a cave. Today, sites of small, temporary fires such as campfires are soon erased by rain and wind or the growth of plants; finding such places from hundreds of thousands, let alone millions, of years ago is a quixotic quest. And while most modern cooking depends on pots and pans, such equipment is far from necessary. Meat or fish can be placed directly on flames or toasted on a stick; roots and tubers and eggs can be baked in hot ash or sand. Humanlike creatures could, therefore, have been tending fires and cooking ages before clear evidence for these activities appears in the archaeological record.

I like to imagine that long before they started cooking, our ancestors were drawn to fire. Some animals are. Birds routinely follow wildfires, often in large numbers, looking to pick off insects and other creatures that are fleeing the flames. And many animals are attracted to areas that have recently burned. Chimpanzees have been spotted sifting through ashes looking for nuts that have been roasted in the conflagration, the roasting having transformed the nuts from something hard and unpalatable to something that can be easily chewed. Rhesus monkeys have been seen eating burned coconuts. In the wake of a wildfire, baboons sometimes snack on cooked grasshoppers. Perhaps at first your ancestors and mine sought out foods that had been charred by bushfire whenever the opportunity arose.

This would not be surprising. Given a choice, chimpanzees and other great apes generally elect to eat cooked food, preferring it to the same food uncooked. Mice prefer cooked food too. Captive chimpanzees have even been observed to keep raw food in reserve, at least for a short time, so that it can be cooked later.

Which makes sense. Cooking is a kind of predigestion: The energy of the fire begins the process of breaking down food. This both increases the availability of nutrients and saves energy when you digest. Eating cooked food thus gives you more calories—more energy—than you could extract from the same food eaten raw. This is true of all foods, but the effect is particularly strong for starchy roots and tubers. Raw, such items are often indigestible. But cooking transforms starch into a far more accessible form. For potatoes, cooking makes starch about twenty times more digestible. Cooked food also requires less chewing, so it is easier and quicker to eat. As an added bonus, cooking kills troublemaking bacteria and other nuisances such as parasitic worms. In other words, cooking not only outsources some of the work of the digestive tract, it doubles as an external immune system, saving you the expense of warding off such troublemakers yourself.

Today, cooking is a feature of all human cultures. As a consequence, humans spend less energy digesting, less time chewing, and far less time eating than other primates do. In fact, humans spend a remarkably short time each day on meals. Although lingering over lunch is a modern delight, if necessary a whole day’s eating can be done in under thirty minutes. In contrast, chimpanzees spend almost seven hours a day eating; gorillas, almost eight. This is not because these animals have nothing else to do but because it’s the only way they can get enough energy from their raw diet. Given that they also sleep for upward of ten hours a day, that doesn’t leave a lot of time for much else.

Modern raw foodists—people who eat most or all of their diet raw—tend to have trouble maintaining their body weight, and also spend a great deal of time preparing food in other ways, for example by blending, pounding, soaking, fermenting, or grinding. Female raw foodists often stop menstruating—meaning that physiologically, they would not be able to support a pregnancy. Note, too, that modern raw foodists eat plants that have been domesticated to be more digestible, and have access to technologies such as electric blenders; without these advantages such a diet would be even harder to sustain.

In short, modern humans have evolved to depend on a cooked diet—and a cooked diet appears to have transformed members of one lineage of hominins into humans. Compared to our ancestors of 2.5 million years ago, humans today have smaller guts, smaller teeth, smaller mouths, weaker jaws—and much larger brains.

The extent to which all these changes coincided with and were permitted by cooking is controversial—much hinges on when cooking started, which is, as I said, unknown. Yet it is hard to see how the large increase in brain size in particular could have happened without it. Today, when you are resting, your brain gobbles up around 20 percent of your energy though it represents only around two percent of your mass. The brains of other primates are far less expensive—consuming perhaps nine percent of the energy of an animal at rest. And although humans are not the largest primates—gorillas are far larger, for example—the human brain has around three times as many neurons as that of a gorilla. Given its raw diet, a gorilla cannot eat enough to support a far bigger brain.

Early experiments with fire may have grown from the discovery that one fire can be used to ignite another: Chimpanzees have been reported to rearrange the smoldering embers of a fire so that they burst back into flame. Back in the days when captive chimpanzees were encouraged to smoke cigarettes, individuals swiftly discovered how to chain-smoke, lighting a new cigarette from the stub of the old. This is distasteful to think about, not least because the animals became nicotine addicts, but it does provide further evidence that chimpanzees can manipulate burning objects with care, precision, and intent. And in Australia today, firehawks—birds of prey such as brown falcons and whistling kites—are said to spread fires by picking up burning twigs and dropping them on unlit vegetation. It’s easy to imagine that the first hominin experiments with ignition began in a similar, fire-lights-fire sort of way.

But the full domestication of fire requires being able to light one from scratch, and that’s trickier, as Charles Darwin discovered. When he visited Tahiti in 1835, he went exploring in the company of local guides. In the evening, after the guides had built “an excellent house” out of bamboo stems, strips of bark, and banana leaves, they began to cook the evening meal. To start the fire, one of the guides rubbed two sticks together. “The fire was produced in a few seconds,” Darwin reported, “but to a person who does not understand the art, it requires, as I found, the greatest exertion.” It also requires the right ingredients. Darwin noted that, in fire making, the Tahitians use only “a peculiarly white and very light wood.”

Without the help of modern aids such as matches, cigarette lighters, or magnifying glasses, there are only two basic ways to start a fire from nothing: rubbing sticks together to generate heat by means of friction, as in Tahiti, or generating sparks by striking stones against one another. In particular, flint—which is made of silica—can be banged against iron pyrite, that mineral also known as fool’s gold. (The word pyrite comes from the Greek for “fire stone.”) The sparks can then be caught by tinder formed from certain fungi or moss or the downy feathers of birds.

Many human cultures have myths and stories to explain their possession of fire. In such accounts, fire is often delivered by an animal. The Dakota people of North America relate that fire was given to them by a mountain lion whose claws gave off sparks as it went springing up the rocks. Other legends tell how a great bison, charging across the plains, set the prairies on fire with the sparks that flew from his hooves. There are tales of toads carrying live coals in their mouths, of fire stolen from vultures, and—in Australia, indeed—of hawks dropping burning twigs. Sometimes, fire has been hidden in a tree—hence the apparently magical effect of rubbing sticks together.

In many of these stories, the benefit of fire is cooking. In some variants, the human discoverer of fire observes another animal cooking and steals an item of cooked food, which is so delicious that the thief becomes inspired to steal fire as well.

Perhaps such stories were first dreamed up around the cooking fires of long ago. But I suspect no one will ever know how or when those early fire creatures discovered reliable methods for making fire: It will forever remain a mystery. Although ancient tools crafted from flint abound, a flint struck against flint does not generate sparks. Further confusing matters, pyrites are not stable in today’s oxygen-rich air, so tangible evidence of their use in fire making may have long since vanished. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

# Archaeologists Just Dug Up an Unused, Completely Pristine 6,000-Year-Old Axe Head

A precious object, not a weapon of war

[DN](https://nautil.us/author/david-nield)

By [David Nield](https://nautil.us/author/david-nield)

7:00 AM CST on November 26, 2026

[Add Nautilus to Google](https://google.com/preferences/source?q=nautil.us)

![Image 4](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/2026/11/01-axe.jpg?w=2880)

Archaeologists have been digging near the Terme di Sorano spa in southern Tuscany since independent archaeologist Stefano Giuntoli noticed a cavity at one of the thermal pools there back in 2024. The subsequent ruins they uncovered have been dated to around 4495–4335 BCE (the Neolithic), and sit on top of an ancient thermal spring. But since the work began, only a few actual objects have been recovered, indicating this was a specialized site, rather than a village or camp where a lot of human activity was happening.

The latest find—a seemingly untouched axe head carved out of greenstone, thought to date back around 6,000 years—further backs up that theory. As the axe head was never used, it’s believed that its presence is symbolic—perhaps used as a part of some kind of religious or spiritual ceremony rather than as a weapon.

![Image 5](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/2026/11/02-site.jpg?w=710)

The axe head where it was found. _Credit: Davide Denci / Terme di Sorano_

Researchers have determined that the axe head is made out of eclogite, a rock formed at great depths and intense pressures. The early European farmers who lived here during the Neolithic may have obtained the carefully crafted piece through trades and exchanges, and ultimately left it as some kind of gift.

[Subscribe to skip ads](https://nautil.us/products)Advertisement

If so, it would be considered a votive offering, which is the act of placing objects in a place for sacred reasons, without any intention of getting them back. It’s possible that the thermal spring was seen as a boundary between worlds.

![Image 6](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/2026/11/03-wide.jpg?w=710)

The wider excavation site. _Credit: Davide Denci / Terme di Sorano_

“The (Terme di Sorano) site is gradually becoming more unique and significant,” Jacopo Francesco Tulipano, one of the team of archaeologists still working at the site, said in a [statement](https://www.intoscana.it/it/terme-di-sorano-nuova-campagna-di-scavo-riaffiora-una-preziosa-ascia-del-neolitico/) (via Google Translate). “The continuation of the work will allow us to gather new data and, once the excavation work is completed, to plan the enhancement of the area.” ![Image 7](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)
